done.why: I hit the 400-turn limit standing in the Smelly Room, partway through the coal-to-diamond plan. The basket with the coal, screwdriver and torch was already lowered down the shaft. My last confirmed score was 154 of 350, and the torch was out of the case at the time.

about: It's a treasure hunt under a white house: find valuables in the caves and haul them back to the trophy case in the living room. This version is different from the one I half-remember in a few pointed ways. The trap door gets barred behind you every time. The studio chimney is the only quick way back up, and it only takes your lamp and one other thing. When you die, your plain things get scattered around the forest and your valuables roll off into dark corners. So the real puzzle is logistics: how to get each treasure back to the case.

moments.note: The troll died in one sword stroke. Much easier than I expected.
The Round Room has cave-ins blocking several of its passages. The map is different from what I remembered.
The thief killed me in one exchange after I attacked him with the sword.
The death message explains where everything went, including that 'somebody tidy has put the lamp back in the living room.' It's funny, and it gave me something to do next.
The platinum bar I lost when I died had 'rolled' into the Studio, right where the death message said valuables would end up.
The chimney refused my load and listed exactly what I carried, then told me the rule: lamp plus one thing. Clear, and it changed how I planned every trip after that.
I tried the chimney with the lit torch as my light, and it explained that the draught would blow out any flame. Nicely reasoned.
Every round trip from the cellar to the case meant chimney, kitchen, living room, trap door, cellar, south, east, north. It got grindy.
The matchbook I'd left in the Studio was gone, probably taken by the thief.
The garlic was still in the sack, so the bat carried me into the coal mine maze.
The coal mine maze is all 'nondescript' rooms, and some exits loop back to the same room. It took about 50 turns of dropping items as markers to map it.
The narrow timber passage named exactly what wouldn't fit, 'anything else bigger than would go in a pocket.' That told me I needed the basket.
Finally found the Gas Room, and a sapphire bracelet was sitting in it.

wished: I wished there were a way out of the cellar that didn't use the chimney while carrying more than one thing. Ferrying one treasure per trip ate most of my turns.
I wished the coal mine rooms had something to tell them apart. I ended up dropping my sack and sword as markers.
I wished I could have fought the thief and lived, or at least had some warning about how deadly he was.
I wished I'd had the turns to finish the diamond machine, the boat and river, the rainbow, and the thief's lair.

lines.line: Your belongings, such as they were, have not come with you. The plain things are strewn about the forest and the fields around the house, anything of value has rolled into some dark corner in or under it, and somebody tidy has put the lamp back in the living room.
lines.why: It made dying into a scavenger hunt, and it turned out to be literally true.

lines.line: The chimney has room for you, your lamp and one thing more, and not an inch besides.
lines.why: This one rule decided how I played the rest of the game.

lines.line: The draught up the chimney would have any flame out before you were halfway, and nothing else you have would see you to the top; it is a climb for a lamp.
lines.why: It's a well-reasoned refusal, and it taught me the torch doesn't count as a lamp.

lines.line: What will not go through the slot between the timbers is the brass lantern, the screwdriver, the small pile of coal, and anything else bigger than would go in a pocket.
lines.why: It told me exactly what the puzzle was without just handing me the answer.

fun.why: Solving the Hades ritual and finding treasures felt great. The repeated chimney round trips and the long stretch in the coal mine maze dragged.

engagement.why: I always knew what I wanted next, and watching the score climb from 35 to 154 kept me hauling treasure even when it was tedious.

difficulty.why: Getting one-shotted by the thief, the narrow chimney and the unmarked maze were hard but fair. Each rule was stated plainly when I ran into it.

interestingness.why: The changes to the familiar game were real and meaningful: the barred trap door, the lamp-only chimney, the scattering on death and the blocked Round Room. They changed how I planned.

prose.why: The new lines are dry and witty, and they explain the rules through the world itself. Everything else reads like the classic text.
